title: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Fiadh's Other Crowd Talk

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Well, here, thank you all for comin..."
entries.text: Well, here, thank you all for coming to listen to me talk. I hear a lot of you have come from far afield...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "So it seems only right that you sho..."
entries.text: So it seems only right that you should get to know this place, our home, a little better.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "We share this land with the Other C..."
entries.text: We share this land with the Other Crowd, the Aos Sí, or People of the Mound. You'll have heard them called many things, no doubt...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "When mankind settled this land, the..."
entries.text: When mankind settled this land, they made a deal with the Fair Folk; they would take half the land, and the Fair Folk would take the other.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Humanity, being tricky, chose the u..."
entries.text: Humanity, being tricky, chose the upper half, and now the Fair Folk live in the Otherworld, parallel to this one.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Still, there's nothing to stop the..."
entries.text: Still, there's nothing to stop the Aos Sí from walking among us, and they often do. You'd always do best to mind them, and be polite to them.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "...Otherwise, they might well cause..."
entries.text: ...Otherwise, they might well cause you trouble. Many have learned the Aos Sí don't take slights kindly, and can give you the worst sort of luck.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Of course, the fair folk have to ha..."
entries.text: Of course, the fair folk have to have means to reach us, and there are plenty of gateways between this world and theirs.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "But they don't all bring bad luck...."
entries.text: But they don't all bring bad luck. Some are only mischievous; some mean well; and some might be bad omens, but they only serve to warn us of ill fate.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "It's not uncommon to find a tree le..."
entries.text: It's not uncommon to find a tree left out in the middle of a farmer's field. Lone hawthorn trees are the meeting place between our world and theirs.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "It's an terrible offence to disturb..."
entries.text: It's an terrible offence to disturb one, and people know better than to try. There are some things in this land that should, by all accounts, be left alone...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Thank you all for coming. I hear a..."
entries.text: Thank you all for coming. I hear a lot of you have come from far afield...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "The fair folk have the means to rea..."
entries.text: The fair folk have the means to reach us, and there are plenty of gateways between this world and theirs.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "So, now we share the land with the..."
entries.text: So, now we share the land with the Aos Sí, the fae - or sometimes, as we call them, the Fair Folk. And while they often live apart from us...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "So there's nothing to stop the Aos..."
entries.text: So there's nothing to stop the Aos Sí from walking among us, and they often do. You'd always do best to mind them, and be polite to them.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "...Otherwise, they might well cause..."
entries.text: ...Otherwise, they might well cause you trouble. Many have learned the Aos Sí don't take slights kindly, and can give you the worst sort of luck.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "They don't all bring bad luck. Some..."
entries.text: They don't all bring bad luck. Some are only mischievous; some mean well; and some might be bad omens, but they only serve to warn us of ill fate.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Either way, they are best left undi..."
entries.text: Either way, they are best left undisturbed. They are one of many things in this land that are not to be meddled with.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "To those of you I haven't met, I'm..."
entries.text: To those of you I haven't met, I'm Fiadh Callaghan, and I'm here to talk to you all about the 'Other Crowd'.

entries.speaker: Detective Ward
entries.label: Decision: "[ STAY AND LISTEN]"
entries.text: [ STAY AND LISTEN]

entries.speaker: Detective Ward
entries.label: Decision: "[ LEAVE ]"
entries.text: [ LEAVE ]

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "If you'll excuse me..."
entries.text: If you'll excuse me...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Well, this is more of a turnout tha..."
entries.text: Well, this is more of a turnout than I was expecting!

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Right. No more questions. I'm tired..."
entries.text: Right. No more questions. I'm tired of trying to talk sense into you lot. Listen or don't. It's no skin off my nose.

entries.speaker: Mister Toussaint
entries.label: Ettiene: "And these fairie--"
entries.text: And these fairie--

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "--please, Sir, don't call them that..."
entries.text: --please, Sir, don't call them that. I've given you many's an alternative that won't draw their eye to this place. Which you don't want, trust me there.

entries.speaker: Mister Toussaint
entries.label: Ettiene: "My apologies, Madame. These Other F..."
entries.text: My apologies, Madame. These Other Folk, they differ from the winged fairies of children's stories, oui?

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "As much as you and I differ from a..."
entries.text: As much as you and I differ from a wild animal, yes.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "All of Europe - probably further -..."
entries.text: All of Europe - probably further - has their own form of the Good Folk. Primordial forces of nature, all. As unknowable to us as a storm or wave.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "As I said, Catholic monks came and..."
entries.text: As I said, Catholic monks came and tainted history. Tried to write them out of existence, and when that failed, they tried to write the fear out of them.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Stories are powerful ways to change..."
entries.text: Stories are powerful ways to change a land and its power. It's why the church always folded in the rituals and beliefs of a place they came to.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "We saw it again in the invasion of..."
entries.text: We saw it again in the invasion of the Americas...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Ah, look, I've lost my train of tho..."
entries.text: Ah, look, I've lost my train of thought with all your questions. Where was I?

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Writing them as friendly winged spr..."
entries.text: Writing them as friendly winged sprites, friendly to children and all that.

entries.speaker: Miss Barbosa
entries.label: Ines: ""Write the fear out of them" - what..."
entries.text: "Write the fear out of them" - what does this mean?

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "And what are they?"
entries.text: And what are they?

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Sure, I can't tell you what nobody..."
entries.text: Sure, I can't tell you what nobody knows.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "But they are more than that... some..."
entries.text: But they are more than that... some would say they are the land incarnate.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Really, it's best to think of them..."
entries.text: Really, it's best to think of them as forces of nature.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "They are no more good or evil than..."
entries.text: They are no more good or evil than a storm. But, you'd also want to stay out of the path of a bad storm.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "All that said, it's easier to avoid..."
entries.text: All that said, it's easier to avoid a storm - there are signs and you get warning. Not so with the Other Folk; best you can do is be polite and leave your offerings.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "And to avoid them altogether? Best..."
entries.text: And to avoid them altogether? Best not to meddle in anything that might catch their eye.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "That's the main reason we don't cal..."
entries.text: That's the main reason we don't call them by their name. Or, you know, do strange magic on their doorstep...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "The church would tie themselves in..."
entries.text: The church would tie themselves in knots trying to bend the truths of the world to fit their narrative...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "They want you to believe, first of..."
entries.text: They want you to believe, first of all, that the Other Crowd don't exist. Then secondly, once you know they are real, the Church wants you to think of them as angels - ones that never took a side in the battle of Heaven.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Cast down to Earth and not Hell for..."
entries.text: Cast down to Earth and not Hell for their sitting on the fence. Now - I've never heard anything of this ilk from any reliable source, only holy salesmen.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Other people confuse them for types..."
entries.text: Other people confuse them for types of ghosts. And given how similar the bean sídhe and fear gorta are to ghosts, I can forgive that.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "What else... Oh yes - speaking of S..."
entries.text: What else... Oh yes - speaking of Samhain... Masks!

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "You all have costumes for the ball..."
entries.text: You all have costumes for the ball this evening, yes?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "It is all good fun, Sì? My outfit w..."
entries.text: It is all good fun, Sì? My outfit will amaze!

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Well, yes. But also... no..."
entries.text: Well, yes. But also... no...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Samhain is when the dead walk among..."
entries.text: Samhain is when the dead walk among us. You know this - sure you're here for that, right?

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Well, when they leave, they don't a..."
entries.text: Well, when they leave, they don't always leave empty-handed. Some want to drag the living with them, jealous as they are.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Maybe. It's certainly been said bef..."
entries.text: Maybe. It's certainly been said before. But just this one year... this one year when you're pushing the barriers to their limits, you might do well to keep a superstition or two in your back pocket.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "That's why we dress up as ghoulish..."
entries.text: That's why we dress up as ghoulish figures  - so they can’t tell the difference between us and them, and will leave us be.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "...I can see some of your faces - s..."
entries.text: ...I can see some of your faces - superstitious old bat, you're thinking.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "...the Good People, the Wee Folk, t..."
entries.text: ...the Good People, the Wee Folk, the Fair Folk. Some of you will know them by the F-word, but we won't be saying that here.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Like in our case, how Ostara became..."
entries.text: Like in our case, how Ostara became Easter, Yule became Christmas, and Samhain became All Souls Day when the blessing of the graves gets done.

title: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Carmela's Ghosts talk

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "There is still much we don't know a..."
entries.text: There is still much we don't know about ghosts, you must think? And this is true - yet there is plenty to speak on, so do not worry! *cough*

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "By their nature... ghosts are hard..."
entries.text: By their nature... ghosts are hard to find and define. And yet, even in their... elusive... ness... Questo funzionerà... we find them everywhere.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "By their many names, they are all a..."
entries.text: By their many names, they are all across the world. They are known all across the world. And how could they not be?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "For whatever we may call them - gho..."
entries.text: For whatever we may call them - ghosts, phantoms, or spirits - there is more to this world than meets the eye, and that is true everywhere you go.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "There are many formations of what w..."
entries.text: There are many formations of what we call ghosts, but mostly, when they are on this side of the veil, we see them in a few forms particularly...

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "So, tomorrow, when the veil is at i..."
entries.text: So, tomorrow, when the veil is at its thinnest... mind your words. These spirits were once people. They are their intangible remains...

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "And they will be just as driven as..."
entries.text: And they will be just as driven as they ever were, if not more.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "We understand ghosts to be the dise..."
entries.text: We understand ghosts to be the disembodied souls of their old selves, sometimes less, or incomplete, as to how they were before.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Or, if not thinking souls, the impr..."
entries.text: Or, if not thinking souls, the imprints of great grief *cough* or strife left upon the world.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "...So, grazie mille, for attending...."
entries.text: ...So, grazie mille, for attending. Now - I will speak with you about ghosts. Spirits! Phantoms!

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Ciao, ciao! For those of you I have..."
entries.text: Ciao, ciao! For those of you I have not yet had the pleasure of meeting, I am Carmela Mantovani. And I am here to talk about ghosts and all that we know of them.

entries.text: [ STAY AND LISTEN ]

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "If you'll excuse me..."
entries.text: If you'll excuse me...

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "So, why do I have such hopes for th..."
entries.text: So, why do I have such hopes for this séance?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "This, I have been doing for a long..."
entries.text: This, I have been doing for a long time. When you invite a ghost to speak with you, there are always limits.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "The strength of the spirit, the ski..."
entries.text: The strength of the spirit, the skill of the medium, the thickness of the veil... All of these things can make it difficult for a ghost to manifest.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "We see their forms on occasion, we..."
entries.text: We see their forms on occasion, we feel the echoes of their emotion, but these things do not require expense. They sustain themselves. Somehow. This we do not understand.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "It takes effort for a spirit to be..."
entries.text: It takes effort for a spirit to be more than echoes, to make a more conscious connection with the world of the living.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "By their nature, they are hard to d..."
entries.text: By their nature, they are hard to define. And yet, even in their... elusive... ness... Questo funzionerà... we find them everywhere!

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "By their many names, they are all a..."
entries.text: By their many names, they are all across the world. There are many formations...

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Some echo the grief they left upon..."
entries.text: Some echo the grief they left upon the world and are blind to the living. *cough*

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "While others are vengeful and aggre..."
entries.text: While others are vengeful and aggressive, haunting a person or place and causing everything from psychological to physical damage!

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Regardless. No single spectre has b..."
entries.text: Regardless. No single spectre has been able to directly communicate.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "But tomorrow night - ah, tomorrow n..."
entries.text: But tomorrow night - ah, tomorrow night we intend to change this!

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "So, what stops them from speaking?..."
entries.text: So, what stops them from speaking? Is it a physical matter? No, it cannot be, as they interact with the world in other ways.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Blowing papers off desks, snuffing..."
entries.text: Blowing papers off desks, snuffing candles, sometimes even striking people. *cough* *cough*

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Perhaps the limitation is in their..."
entries.text: Perhaps the limitation is in their lungs, then? Well, no, many wail and moan after all.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Maybe they simply cannot speak for..."
entries.text: Maybe they simply cannot speak for themselves?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Could it be they have nothing to sa..."
entries.text: Could it be they have nothing to say?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "I do not think so. Many a mystic, m..."
entries.text: I do not think so. Many a mystic, myself included, believe that spirits have given us a feeling of things they want said.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "There is a chance this is wishful t..."
entries.text: There is a chance this is wishful thinking on our parts, but I believe so many have felt this that at least one person must be correct...

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "This, we cannot rule out, and is to..."
entries.text: This, we cannot rule out, and is to be my conclusion if our séance does not bear fruit.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "We think of ghosts as waveforms. Sp..."
entries.text: We think of ghosts as waveforms. Spiritual waveforms. A soul rippling long past the death of its host, its shell.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "They are in a frequency we cannot e..."
entries.text: They are in a frequency we cannot easily see. In daytime, they are almost invisible to us.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "This is an *cough* age of science,..."
entries.text: This is an *cough* age of science, yes? So let me speak in those terms.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "At night, easier to see. The less....."
entries.text: At night, easier to see. The less... interference around - lights, other people, and so on - the easier, still.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "If you have noticed animals behavin..."
entries.text: If you have noticed animals behaving strangely, this is because they see different wavelengths to us, as is with light.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "The atmosphere blocks the wavelengt..."
entries.text: The atmosphere blocks the wavelength of light. The same is true for spiritual wavelengths.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "But at this time of year, the veil..."
entries.text: But at this time of year, the veil - or spiritual atmosphere - is at its thinnest.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "And this place is reported to have..."
entries.text: And this place is reported to have many ghosts. So our wavelengths have less distance to travel and less to block them.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "And then, there is you. Those gathe..."
entries.text: And then, there is you. Those gathered. People attuned to the mystical, coming together to work as a... qual è la parola? A net to catch the signal.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "No, net is not correct. Che cos'è?..."
entries.text: No, net is not correct. Che cos'è? Ah, my words let me down. But look, if you do not believe me?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "I'm told that crows are a symbol of..."
entries.text: I'm told that crows are a symbol of your Irish death-goddess. They are gathering! And at night, the dead are roaming - I think they line up for the chance to speak to us!

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "In parting, a warning."
entries.text: In parting, a warning.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "We do know that not all dead linger..."
entries.text: We do know that not all dead linger - only those bound to a place, an object, a person stay. Why? This, eh, this we do not know yet for certain.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "It is theorised that all spirits ar..."
entries.text: It is theorised that all spirits are bound, fettered, by an emotional component - death in a place, obsession with an object, love or anger to a person.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "And then, there is you. Those gathe..."
entries.text: And then, there is you. Those gathered. Do I describe you as a way to boost the wavelength or as a way to widen the signal receiver?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "I do not know, but the effect is th..."
entries.text: I do not know, but the effect is the same. And if you don't believe me?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "I'm told that crows are a symbol of..."
entries.text: I'm told that crows are a symbol of The Morrigan, the Irish death-goddess. They are gathering! And at night the dead are roaming - I think they line up for the chance to speak to us!

title: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/coventry on the region

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Well. This is quite the turnout. Ev..."
entries.text: Well. This is quite the turnout. Even the Marquess himself has come. Well...

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "I hadn't expected anyone to take mu..."
entries.text: I hadn't expected anyone to take much interest in the area.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "I suppose I should start by introdu..."
entries.text: I suppose I should start by introducing myself. My name is Simon Coventry.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "I'm going to share some interesting..."
entries.text: I'm going to share some interesting facts about this part of Ireland that I picked up while researching for this trip.

entries.speaker: Detective Ward
entries.label: Decision: "[ STAY AND LISTEN ]"
entries.text: [ STAY AND LISTEN ]

entries.speaker: Detective Ward
entries.label: Decision: "[ LEAVE ]"
entries.text: [ LEAVE ]

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "Please excuse me."
entries.text: Please excuse me.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "So, I am sure you all know this lan..."
entries.text: So, I am sure you all know this land came into the Blake family in the 1650s after Cromwell's invasion.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "What I found interesting was what c..."
entries.text: What I found interesting was what came before...

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "This land was a place of worship an..."
entries.text: This land was a place of worship and innovation.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "I couldn't find anything that spoke..."
entries.text: I couldn't find anything that spoke to what happened at the work from that site - presumably it was set ablaze.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "One has to assume not everyone was..."
entries.text: One has to assume not everyone was put to death by Cromwell's forces, however...

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "I suspect many surrounding families..."
entries.text: I suspect many surrounding families have stories and knowledge passed down from that time and those people.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Why, given his background, perhaps..."
entries.text: Why, given his background, perhaps our very own Doctor Callaghan is linked to that place?

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Ha, you flatter me, Sir."
entries.text: Ha, you flatter me, Sir.

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "Does anything of the pre-Christian..."
entries.text: Does anything of the pre-Christian site still exist?

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "I read one monk's account that what..."
entries.text: I read one monk's account that what was here before was partially underground.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "There are some sinkholes on the far..."
entries.text: There are some sinkholes on the far reaches of the grounds, where caverns beneath the old settlements collapsed in.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "I do not know whether those collaps..."
entries.text: I do not know whether those collapses are the result of time or if they were manually closed.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "I suppose it matters not either way..."
entries.text: I suppose it matters not either way. Nothing else remains.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "That's me, I am afraid. I've nothin..."
entries.text: That's me, I am afraid. I've nothing else to share.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Probably quite mundane in the face..."
entries.text: Probably quite mundane in the face of everything, but nothing wrong with a break in the face of madness!

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Perhaps those survivors are the rea..."
entries.text: Perhaps those survivors are the reason that Connacht is home to all manner of wonderful myths and sacred sites?

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Rathcroghan and Oweynagat cave, Que..."
entries.text: Rathcroghan and Oweynagat cave, Queen Medb and her cattle raids, the Children of Lir - all fascinating stories, but too long to get into here.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "A gathering spot for scholars and e..."
entries.text: A gathering spot for scholars and engineers, and artists to work on understanding and advancement - the betterment of their people.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Easy pickings for Edward Blake. No..."
entries.text: Easy pickings for Edward Blake. No doubt he and Cromwell cared very little for any knowledge held by 'primitive pagans'...

entries.speaker: Missus D'Arcy
entries.label: DArcy: "Thank you Marquess. I wanted to ask..."
entries.text: Thank you Marquess. I wanted to ask about the land before your family came here - is it true this was a sacred site?

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "Before my family brought culture an..."
entries.text: Before my family brought culture and civilisation, Sir, every tree, stone, and river was sacred to the savage pagans of these lands.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "But you are right, this was a place..."
entries.text: But you are right, this was a place of particular significance.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "It was said to be home to their god..."
entries.text: It was said to be home to their god of innovation and medicine.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "It brought many of their finest min..."
entries.text: It brought many of their finest minds to the area, whatever bar for quality that could mean.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "I suspect this played large part in..."
entries.text: I suspect this played large part in Cromwell ordering it raised to the ground and built over. As both a statement and to consecrate the land in God's glory.

entries.speaker: Mister Skerritt
entries.label: Skerritt: "Perhaps things would have turned ou..."
entries.text: Perhaps things would have turned out better for them had this been a shrine to ones of their war gods, eh? Hahaha!

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "...indeed."
entries.text: ...indeed.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "I could find no knowledge of what h..."
entries.text: I could find no knowledge of what happened to any of the work from that site, presumably it was set ablaze.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Oh... I don't think so, I am afraid..."
entries.text: Oh... I don't think so, I am afraid. From what I can gather, it was all razed to make way for the castle and its estate.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Well! There you go, Father."
entries.text: Well! There you go, Father.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "You've done your homework, Father...."
entries.text: You've done your homework, Father. Yes, some accounts do suggest that - though none of the maps I've studied show anything useful. Marquess?

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Certainly worth a read in the very..."
entries.text: Certainly worth a read in the very well-stocked library here, if you find yourself bored - not that I can see that happening with the séance only hours away!

entries.text: Of course, the Great Famine was hard on much of Ireland.

entries.label: JBlake: "And we were no exception."
entries.text: And we were no exception.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake

entries.text: Those were hard years on the land and our family.

entries.text: My father sold much of the estate and made some... daring investments across Europe.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake

entries.text: They did not pay off.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "And so, when I was of age and title..."
entries.text: And so, when I was of age and title, I turned the manor into a hotel.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "What remains of the land is still f..."
entries.text: What remains of the land is still farmed or forested, of course.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "If you'll excuse me..."
entries.text: If you'll excuse me...

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "Welcome, all of you, to my home. I..."
entries.text: Welcome, all of you, to my home. I am Jonathan Blake, the Marquess of Doon, lord of this manor, and all the land that can be seen from it.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "I have been asked to speak with you..."
entries.text: I have been asked to speak with you about the house and its history, which dates back to 1652.

entries.speaker: Detective Ward

entries.text: [ STAY AND LISTEN]

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "My ancestor, Edward Blake, was gran..."
entries.text: My ancestor, Edward Blake, was granted this land in the winter of 1651. The following summer, work began on the castle that, in turn, became this manor.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "You Sir, a question?"
entries.text: You Sir, a question?

entries.speaker: Mister Skerritt
entries.label: Skerritt: "Thank you, Marquess. Not to turn th..."
entries.text: Thank you, Marquess. Not to turn things gruesome, but is it true? What they say about the walled-up rooms?

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "..."

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "As such we continue to display a po..."
entries.text: As such we continue to display a portrait of Percival Blake. That said, I did have it moved from the main halls on the staff's request. Now it is in one of the towers, though I can't recall which.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "Certainly, it is rumoured that Perc..."
entries.text: Certainly, it is rumoured that Percival Blake bricked away two young lovers for angering him.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "Set across from one another, so the..."
entries.text: Set across from one another, so they could hear each other's final days.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "That said, no such chambers were fo..."
entries.text: That said, no such chambers were found, nor records of work being done that match the timing.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "It is true that a young couple did..."
entries.text: It is true that a young couple did indeed vanish with no record, but that wasn't uncommon for that era.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "Over the years, some staff, and yes..."
entries.text: Over the years, some staff, and yes, even guests, have reported hearing sobs from a young woman in the east of the manor. But given the lack of evidence, these are likely flights of fancy.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "The building has been expanded many..."
entries.text: The building has been expanded many times over since then, and you would be hard-pressed to tell the original building and the additions apart.

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "But the main compound has roughly e..."
entries.text: But the main compound has roughly expanded to five times its original size. This is not counting the basement, which was added in the late 1700s.

entries.speaker: Missus D'Arcy
entries.label: DArcy: "Thank you Marquess. Any more tragic..."
entries.text: Thank you Marquess. Any more tragic deaths to share?

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "...No more questions? Okay. Let us..."
entries.text: ...No more questions? Okay. Let us conclude then. Thank you all for your time.

entries.speaker: Missus D'Arcy

entries.text: Then why all the ghost stories? I don't think we all gathered here for no reason...

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "Spending too much time digging arou..."

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake

entries.speaker: Marquess Blake
entries.label: JBlake: "I shall take my leave, but I hope y..."

entries.text: That's perhaps a better question for Miss Mantovani...

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "The Blake family once owned all the..."
entries.text: The Blake family once owned all the land in this area. 20,000 acres was assigned to them, or 35 square miles. Even now all you can see from this manor still belongs to the family.

entries.speaker: Mister Coventry
entries.label: Coventry: "Of course, much of this land isn't..."
entries.text: Of course, much of this land isn't particularly farmable, so what was missing in quality was made up in quantity.

title: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Ruairí's mythology talk

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Good afternoon, ladies and gentleme..."
entries.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I am Doctor Ruairí Callaghan, and I'm pleased to see you all here.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "I'd like to give my thanks, first o..."
entries.text: I'd like to give my thanks, first of all - to you good people for attending this talk of mine, and to the Marquess for inviting me to speak.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "I’m going to talk to you today abou..."
entries.text: I’m going to talk to you today about the mythology of Ireland - the generations of mythical figures that were said to walk this land before us…

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "…and the story of our forefathers,..."
entries.text: …and the story of our forefathers, as legend tells it, and how they secured our place here on this small part of the planet that we call home.

entries.speaker: Detective Ward
entries.label: Decision: "[ STAY AND LISTEN ]"
entries.text: [ STAY AND LISTEN ]

entries.speaker: Detective Ward
entries.label: Decision: "[ LEAVE ]"
entries.text: [ LEAVE ]

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "If you would excuse me..."
entries.text: If you would excuse me...

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "It will help you to understand that..."
entries.text: It will help you to understand that there are four cycles in Irish mythology. First, there is the Mythological Cycle.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "It concerns the most ancient reache..."
entries.text: It concerns the most ancient reaches of our mythology, a time when a godlike race, the Tuatha De Danann...

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Secondly, there is the Ulster Cycle..."
entries.text: Secondly, there is the Ulster Cycle, which took place around the birth of Christ.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "It mostly concerns the warfare of t..."
entries.text: It mostly concerns the warfare of the regional kingdoms that made up what we now know as Ireland.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "The third cycle is the Fenian Cycle..."
entries.text: The third cycle is the Fenian Cycle, which focuses less on gods and their ilk, or even royalty. It concerns itself with exploits of hunters and bards, especially the Fianna, led by the hero Fionn Mac Cumhaill.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "And finally, there is the fourth cy..."
entries.text: And finally, there is the fourth cycle - the Cycle of Kings. This cycle, as you may guess, tells the story of the kings of Ireland, often with a moral to their story about the qualities that are desirable – or undesirable – in a king.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "The fourth cycle is also that in wh..."
entries.text: The fourth cycle is also that in which we find the story of the Milesians, our forefathers, those who would win a battle against the Tuatha Dé Danann.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "...shared this land with the Aos Sí..."
entries.text: ...shared this land with the Aos Sí or the Fair Folk - on which my aunt has already spoken to you.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "…Even after the first cycle, where..."
entries.text: …Even after the first cycle, where they are seen most often, the Tuatha Dé Danann occur in many tales throughout Irish mythology.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "…Which brings me to the Milesians."
entries.text: …Which brings me to the Milesians.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Thank you all so much for listening..."
entries.text: Thank you all so much for listening.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "They are not gods in the Christian..."
entries.text: They are not gods in the Christian sense – they do not have the same level of power, nor are they all-knowing.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Rather, they are more akin to the g..."
entries.text: Rather, they are more akin to the gods found in Ancient Greece or Rome.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "They are understood to have dominio..."
entries.text: They are understood to have dominion over certain aspects of life, yes.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "But they were also understood to ex..."
entries.text: But they were also understood to exist in a form possible for mortals to encounter, and bound by degrees of the practical nature this implies.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Their plans, as we find in these my..."
entries.text: Their plans, as we find in these myths, can be waylaid or circumvented by wily heroes.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Ireland herself is often seen incar..."
entries.text: Ireland herself is often seen incarnate in the Fourth Cycle as a bride to a worthy king, demonstrating how the figures found in the narrative and the ideas they embody can become enmeshed...

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "...And how, immortal as the ideas a..."
entries.text: ...And how, immortal as the ideas and domains of the Tuatha Dé Danann are, their kind can still be harmed, defeated, or even killed by adversaries - whomsoever those may be.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "The immortal nature of their domain..."
entries.text: The immortal nature of their domain, too, means that while we now live in a more enlightened age, we must not be so quick to dismiss these stories as entirely fantasy.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Where the heart of a story has bear..."
entries.text: Where the heart of a story has bearing in reality, you will often find some surrounding elements do, too.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "It may be that some of the stories..."
entries.text: It may be that some of the stories we find in the mythological cycles are the accounts of actual happenings, made legendary through their retelling.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "This holds particular weight when o..."
entries.text: This holds particular weight when one considers that we all know an element of the stories' supernatural aspects - being here as magicians ourselves, to speak with the dead - to be entirely plausible, if not demonstrably true.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "The Milesians - our ancestors, at l..."
entries.text: The Milesians - our ancestors, at least for those Irish in the room - did not start their story in Ireland, but were a group of people who had travelled the Earth for many hundreds of years.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "They came from Iberia, first led by..."
entries.text: They came from Iberia, first led by a man named Íth, who met with the three high kings of Ireland - members of the Tuatha Dé Danann.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "He also met his end in Ireland, tho..."
entries.text: He also met his end in Ireland, though the myths do not agree as to who or what killed him.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Regardless, descendants of his brot..."
entries.text: Regardless, descendants of his brother’s line - the three brothers Amergin, Éremon, and Éber Finn - would later come to Ireland, seeking vengeance for Íth’s death.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "To do so, their forces travelled to..."
entries.text: To do so, their forces travelled to the royal capital of Ireland to confront the kings he held responsible for their uncle’s demise.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Along the way, his party met three..."
entries.text: Along the way, his party met three goddesses - Banba, Fódhla, and Ériu -the wives of the three high kings, all of them both goddesses and embodiments of the land - a motif we discussed earlier.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Each of them promised that they wou..."
entries.text: Each of them promised that they would bring them good luck, if they would only name the land after them.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "The Milesians and the high kings ne..."
entries.text: The Milesians and the high kings negotiated a truce, in which the Milesians would stay three days anchored offshore in their fleet -

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "But it was a trick! The Tuatha Dé D..."
entries.text: But it was a trick! The Tuatha Dé Danann conjured a storm to wreck their foe's fleet.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "However, Amergin was a legendary po..."
entries.text: However, Amergin was a legendary poet, and calmed the winds with magical verse.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Those ships that outlasted the stor..."
entries.text: Those ships that outlasted the storms took again to land, and - after great wars were waged - the survivors negotiated their peace.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "When offered half of the land, the..."
entries.text: When offered half of the land, the Milesians agreed - and cunningly took the upper half, relegating the Tuatha Dé Danann to the Otherworld below.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "The land above was divided by Amerg..."
entries.text: The land above was divided by Amergin between his brothers, giving the north to Éremon and the south to Éber Finn.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "They became the new high kings of I..."
entries.text: They became the new high kings of Ireland - then known in the Irish tongue as Éire, in tribute to one of the sovereignty goddesses of old.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "I hope this gives you an understand..."
entries.text: I hope this gives you an understanding of where we've come from. Of the kinds of people we are.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "It concerns the most ancient reache..."
entries.text: It concerns the most ancient reaches of our mythology, a time when a godlike race, the Tuatha De Danann...

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "... also known as the Aos Sí or the..."
entries.text: ... also known as the Aos Sí or the Fair Folk - as my aunt has already spoken of to you - were the primary inhabitants of the land.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "Indeed, many is the god that has di..."
entries.text: Indeed, many is the god that has died at human hands. Or close enough to how we see death for it to be functionally the same in our eyes.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "They became the new high kings of I..."
entries.text: They became the new high kings of Ireland - named under their rule, in the Irish tongue, Éire, after one of the goddesses that had so decreed it.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "I hope you might better understand..."
entries.text: I hope you might better understand this place now; that you might appreciate it more keenly, whether you are of this land or not.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "A people who cannot be wiped out, w..."
entries.text: A people who cannot be wiped out, who can overcome any force and the tricks they may use.

entries.speaker: Doctor Callaghan
entries.label: Ruairí: "A people who will not stop until th..."
entries.text: A people who will not stop until this land is theirs once more.

title: Ground floor/Drawing Room/comments from NPCs/Dupré's global stage talk

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Good afternoon, everyone, and welco..."
entries.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "If I have not yet had the pleasure..."
entries.text: If I have not yet had the pleasure of making your acquaintance, then please let me introduce myself.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "My name is Lloyd Dupré, and I am ho..."
entries.text: My name is Lloyd Dupré, and I am honoured to have this opportunity to speak with you all.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "My topic today will be the gods of..."
entries.text: My topic today will be the gods of Ireland, how gods can be adopted and changed by their uptake across the world...

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "And what it is that inspires the co..."
entries.text: And what it is that inspires the continued worship of a god, even when they may no longer be in their original context and form.

entries.speaker: Detective Ward
entries.label: Decision: "[ STAY AND LISTEN ]"
entries.text: [ STAY AND LISTEN ]

entries.speaker: Detective Ward
entries.label: Decision: "[ LEAVE ]"
entries.text: [ LEAVE ]

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "Excuse me."
entries.text: Excuse me.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "First of all, we’ll discuss the god..."
entries.text: First of all, we’ll discuss the gods native to Ireland, worshipped before the adoption of Christianity in the region.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "I’m afraid we won’t have time to ta..."
entries.text: I’m afraid we won’t have time to talk about them all, as there are many, and many of them have quite extensive myths…

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "But we will talk about some of the..."
entries.text: But we will talk about some of the foremost among them.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "The Mórrigan is a goddess in three..."
entries.text: The Mórrigan is a goddess in three parts, sometimes referred to as a singular woman, sometimes as three sisters...

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Or sometimes as a singular goddess..."
entries.text: Or sometimes as a singular goddess with three distinct aspects.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "No matter which form she is thought..."
entries.text: No matter which form she is thought to take, she is a fearsome goddess; one thought to hold the domains of battle, and thusly victory and doom.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "She is a guardian of the battlefiel..."
entries.text: She is a guardian of the battlefield, inspiring bravery in warriors and terror in their enemies.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "And perhaps due to her close link t..."
entries.text: And perhaps due to her close link to death through battle, she is often associated with the crow - even appearing as one in certain myths.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Lesser known, perhaps because she s..."
entries.text: Lesser known, perhaps because she seems more unique to the more northern European experience, is the Cailleach.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "She is recognised across the Britis..."
entries.text: She is recognised across the British Isles - not as an exact copy, of course - but with recognisable similarities.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "She is understood to be a “hag”, a..."
entries.text: She is understood to be a “hag”, a goddess in the form of an older woman to symbolise wisdom.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "And she is another fearsome goddess..."
entries.text: And she is another fearsome goddess at that, well respected, but considered to have power over storms and winter... so not one you want to displease.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "There are other gods, too, with dom..."
entries.text: There are other gods, too, with domains less directly tied to the natural world and instead to society.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Goibniu, the smith god, was a much..."
entries.text: Goibniu, the smith god, was a much respected figure and, with a secondary domain of hospitality, was intrinsically tied to societal aspects of life.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "The goddess Brigid, beside him also..."
entries.text: The goddess Brigid, beside him also had some domain over smithcraft, though her associations were more widely spread.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "She was thought to be a goddess of..."
entries.text: She was thought to be a goddess of smithing, but also of poetry and healing - each attributed to one of the "sisters".

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "It is Brigid I wish to focus on, fo..."
entries.text: It is Brigid I wish to focus on, for now, as she provides a wonderful example of how mythology and religion may be adopted across the world.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Like the goddess Mórrigan, she was..."
entries.text: Like the goddess Mórrigan, she was sometimes said to have two sisters, though this may also be interpreted as her having a three-fold, or “triplicate” form.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Where I am from, the city of New Or..."
entries.text: Where I am from, the city of New Orleans in the state of Louisiana, itself in the United States of America, there can be seen a unique mythology and religion.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "North America is a primarily Christ..."
entries.text: North America is a primarily Christian country.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "However, as I’m sure you’re aware,..."
entries.text: However, as I’m sure you’re aware, before the Abolitionary Act of 1865, a great many people were displaced from their homes by slavers.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "These people brought with them thei..."
entries.text: These people brought with them their cultures, and the gods and the worship they were accustomed to.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "One of these figures of worship was..."
entries.text: One of these figures of worship was the Loa, the spirit, Maman Brigitte. Does the name sound familiar?

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "The truth is, that as they were una..."
entries.text: The truth is, that as they were unable to worship openly, practitioners of voodoo took to worshipping Saints found in the Catholic tradition, the Saints being guises for their Loas.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "This is a practice called syncretis..."
entries.text: This is a practice called syncretism, combining schools of religious thought.  Maman Brigitte is worshipped, if not as herself, occasionally as Mary Magdalene…

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "But more often, as Saint Brigid of..."
entries.text: But more often, as Saint Brigid of Kildare, the Christian interpretation of the goddess Brigid, for their shared association with fire and snakes.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "It is my opinion that characters of..."
entries.text: It is my opinion that characters of gods hold particular sway across the world if they have a domain that is common to the human experience.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "And while we no longer live in an a..."
entries.text: And while we no longer live in an age of warriors and great battles, such as that the Mórrigan was said to oversee…

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Now, Maman Brigitte is the guardian..."
entries.text: Now, Maman Brigitte is the guardian of cemeteries and the dead, and she protects those who have been laid to rest...

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Bríd, goddess of poets, would surel..."
entries.text: Bríd, goddess of poets, would surely still have domain with the authors of our age...

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "And one must imagine the spirit of..."
entries.text: And one must imagine the spirit of Giobniu would be found in the Industrial Revolution that makes so much possible.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "The domains of gods are not lost, n..."
entries.text: The domains of gods are not lost, not to those that would worship them. They simply change.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Across time and continents, their d..."
entries.text: Across time and continents, their domains still hold meaning even if they take forms we no longer recognise. Such is the nature of things.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Dear guests, I would like to thank..."
entries.text: Dear guests, I would like to thank each and every one of you for attending.

entries.speaker: Mister Dupré
entries.label: Dupré: "Feel free to chat with me later if..."
entries.text: Feel free to chat with me later if you have any further questions.

entries.label: FatherSinnott: "Miles inside its interior, I saw an..."
entries.text: Miles inside its interior, I saw an altar of ice. The answer, I knew, was there.

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "We left at once, but it took months..."
entries.text: We left at once, but it took months of digging, climbing, and searching to find the frozen shrine, buried far beyond what von Posselt-Czorich had discovered of the caves.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "..."

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "Worry not, child. I see the look in..."
entries.text: Worry not, child. I see the look in your eye. The fear of killing such a being.

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "But you can only kill its mortal sh..."
entries.text: But you can only kill its mortal shell, that which is used to anchor it to this place.

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "In truth, all you will do is set it..."
entries.text: In truth, all you will do is set it free!

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "And once freed, it will return to M..."
entries.text: And once freed, it will return to Monad and tell them of this place, this realm of rot and debauchery.

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "Once the True God knows of us and o..."
entries.text: Once the True God knows of us and our plight in this prison, and of our dedication and kindness in freeing Its Aeon, It will come - It will save us.

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "And we will be free!"
entries.text: And we will be free!

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "Now... If you could excuse me. I......"
entries.text: Now... If you could excuse me. I... am so tired. I do not think I have this evening's séance in me.

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "Perhaps... you can succeed where Se..."
entries.text: Perhaps... you can succeed where Seamus and I have failed.

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "Go, child. Find the Aeon and free i..."
entries.text: Go, child. Find the Aeon and free it. Free us all...

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "It was not so grand now, having mel..."
entries.text: It was not so grand now, having melted after who knows how long. But there I found it...

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "Behold!"
entries.text: Behold!

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "I am not sure... I have much left i..."
entries.text: I am not sure... I have much left in me... at all...

entries.speaker: Father Sinnott
entries.label: FatherSinnott: "And now... Seamus is gone..."
entries.text: And now... Seamus is gone...

title: Outside/Graveyard/conversations/arwa and cathal

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "...over a hundred years ago, a vase..."
entries.text: ...over a hundred years ago, a vase was unearthed from an unidentified tomb in what used to be Nubia. It was found with the canopic jars.

entries.speaker: Mister O'Meara
entries.label: Cathal: "Rotted away?"
entries.text: Rotted away?

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "No. There are mummified hearts that..."
entries.text: No. There are mummified hearts that have lasted thousands of years. And the jar was still sealed.

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "The distinction is, to be particula..."
entries.text: The distinction is, to be particular, that archaeologists study physical objects. But much of it is found buried, yes.

entries.speaker: Mister O'Meara
entries.label: Cathal: "And that is where you found those j..."
entries.text: And that is where you found those jars for me?

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "It took the place, among the set, o..."
entries.text: It took the place, among the set, of the jar that would have held the entombed's heart - and yet, it was empty.

entries.speaker: Mister O'Meara
entries.label: Cathal: "And whose tomb was it?"
entries.text: And whose tomb was it?

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "It was unmarked. Unknown."
entries.text: It was unmarked. Unknown.

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "Likely, whoever was buried there wi..."
entries.text: Likely, whoever was buried there wished to be unknown... or forgotten.

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "In short, yes. But I was on the hun..."
entries.text: In short, yes. But I was on the hunt for something else - a vase.

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "I think it was the real final resti..."
entries.text: I think it was the real final resting place of Nectanebo II.

entries.speaker: Mister O'Meara
entries.label: Cathal: "Oh?"
entries.text: Oh?

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "His royal sarcophagus was never use..."
entries.text: His royal sarcophagus was never used. He fled after defeat by the Persians and ended up in...

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "Yes, exactly this. Notably, he was..."
entries.text: Yes, exactly this. Notably, he was considered to be a powerful magician.

entries.speaker: Mister O'Meara
entries.label: Cathal: "So you suspect the missing heart is..."
entries.text: So you suspect the missing heart is related to that?

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "I do not think the heart was missin..."
entries.text: I do not think the heart was missing. I think... perhaps it was destroyed in some ritual of his?

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "Thanks to our Miss Deane, I now kno..."
entries.text: Thanks to our Miss Deane, I now know the last documented person to have had the vase - Barnard Blake. A great-granduncle of the Marquess, though he never held the title himself.

entries.speaker: Mister O'Meara
entries.label: Cathal: "And you think your vase... it is he..."
entries.text: And you think your vase... it is here?

entries.speaker: Miss Hisham
entries.label: Arwa: "This is where my trail ends. So I a..."
entries.text: This is where my trail ends. So I am hopeful. But I have searched this place as much as I can - there is only the basement and the residence.

entries.speaker: Mister O'Meara
entries.label: Cathal: "Well, good luck to you. If I can he..."
entries.text: Well, good luck to you. If I can help, I will. I am indebted for the jars.

title: Outside/Hedge Maze/Conversations/Fiadh scrying with Carmela

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani

entries.text: Andiamo, little well. You show me nothing!

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Don't go getting worked up about it..."
entries.text: Don't go getting worked up about it, now, or you won't get anywhere. Scrying is a delicate art.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Tsk! I am focused! I am a magician,..."
entries.text: Tsk! I am focused! I am a magician, and a very good one - this should not be hard for me!

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "None of that. You're better than th..."
entries.text: None of that. You're better than that, aren't you? Don't let pride cloud your mind. You're focused, perhaps, but on what?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "My family, of course!"
entries.text: My family, of course!

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Except… No. When I think of them, I..."
entries.text: Except… No. When I think of them, I imagine what these people would say of me... Leaving them as I did...

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "…You put too much on yourself."
entries.text: …You put too much on yourself.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Hah! Santo cielo - says she, carrie..."
entries.text: Hah! Santo cielo - says she, carrier of woes.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Well, I’d rather carry woes than ex..."
entries.text: Well, I’d rather carry woes than expectations.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "Sometimes we just need to put down..."
entries.text: Sometimes we just need to put down the load, Carmela.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Oh, I see them. Ah, but I forgot ho..."
entries.text: Oh, I see them. Ah, but I forgot how good it feels to see them. It has been so long, and I am so far from home...

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "Ah, cielo. Is that rain?"
entries.text: Ah, cielo. Is that rain?

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "…Oh."
entries.text: …Oh.

entries.speaker: Miss Mantovani
entries.label: Carmela: "But what choice did I have? A magic..."
entries.text: But what choice did I have? A magician must glitter! Whatever mud she is born in, she must bloom and escape to survive!

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "The mind must be relaxed, but focus..."
entries.text: The mind must be relaxed, but focused. Not so easy, at least not at first.

entries.text: You said that just the way my sister talks about her children, you know.

entries.text: I only said she'll be fourteen.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan

entries.text: It's not the words, dear, but the tone. Just the way a parent would talk about their child.

entries.speaker: Miss Quinn
entries.label: Corentine: "It so happens I might be the closes..."
entries.text: It so happens I might be the closest Alma has, these days.

entries.speaker: Miss Callaghan
entries.label: Fiadh: "That's a terrible burden for someon..."
entries.text: That's a terrible burden for someone so young.

entries.speaker: Miss Quinn
entries.label: Corentine: "No. It's a privilege. I hope I get..."
entries.text: No. It's a privilege. I hope I get to continue it.

entries.speaker: Miss Quinn
entries.label: Corentine: "No. It's a privilege. One that I am..."
entries.text: No. It's a privilege. One that I am happy that I'll now get to fulfil to its end.

entries.text: "Even my own flesh and blood didn't know me! In hindsight, I was probably memorable enough - a wealthy outsider coming to ask of their god."

entries.text: "My back is in agony today, for it. I have taken most of a bottle to ease the pain."

entries.text: A collection of papers, a birth certificate, and a journal...

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "It's the birth certificate of a Hen..."
entries.text: It's the birth certificate of a Henry Blake, who seems to be the older cousin of Jonathan Blake. The actual heir to the title and lands, here.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "His father died when he was still a..."
entries.text: His father died when he was still a young lad. Rather than pass the title and lands to Henry, an attempt was made on his life by Jonathan Blake's father.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "Henry's mother took him and fled. S..."
entries.text: Henry's mother took him and fled. She died soon after, leaving him alone in the world.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "That is where he discovered Goibniu..."
entries.text: That is where he discovered Goibniu, locked in a deep sleep.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "And, eventually, much older he retu..."
entries.text: And, eventually, much older he returned to the manor, armed with an understanding of the grounds' secrets.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "He had adopted the identity of Simo..."
entries.text: He had adopted the identity of Simon Coventry - a man who had also recently lost his wife.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "Over this, he bonded with the Marqu..."
entries.text: Over this, he bonded with the Marquess and used that to gain the access he needed to search the grounds.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "All he had were his father's notes,..."
entries.text: All he had were his father's notes, the notes that resulted in his death. Among them, the sigil.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "He spent much of his life studying..."
entries.text: He spent much of his life studying the occult to make sense of the sigil.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "The god's dreams already coloured b..."
entries.text: The god's dreams already coloured by the events happening around him.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "He found the chamber his father had..."
entries.text: He found the chamber his father had died opening and was able to get inside.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "Coventry took advantage of this thr..."
entries.text: Coventry took advantage of this through prayer and something he calls his "shrine of images".

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "The Marquess will kill himself, thi..."
entries.text: The Marquess will kill himself, thinking he both kills and frees his son.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "Then, with Blake gone and the god f..."
entries.text: Then, with Blake gone and the god freed, Coventry will ask for his reward - to have his youth returned.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "He will then take his place as the..."
entries.text: He will then take his place as the heir in the form of Walter Blake - the son with paintings, documents, and mesmerised staff to vouch for him as the next-in-line to the title.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "And Goibniu's dreams reshaped the m..."
entries.text: And Goibniu's dreams reshaped the minds of everyone around him into thinking there was a Walter Blake, who's been crippled in the accident that killed his mother.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "The god's dream can't force anyone..."
entries.text: The god's dream can't force anyone to act outside of their interest. He couldn't be made to kill himself, but he could be tricked into doing it for the right reason.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "Because, to unlock the gate, he nee..."
entries.text: Because, to unlock the gate, he needs Blake blood - a result of their ending up as third Milesian bloodline through Edward Blake's awful actions.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "Because, to unlock the gate, he nee..."
entries.text: Because, to unlock the gate, he needs Blake blood - it says here they are the last of the third Milesian bloodline.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward
entries.label: Ward: "That is where he discovered the Ent..."
entries.text: That is where he discovered the Entity, locked in a deep sleep.

entries.speaker: Mister Ward

entries.text: And its dreams reshaped the minds of everyone around him into thinking there was a Walter Blake, who's been crippled in the accident that killed his mother.

title: Document Texts/Hiring Telegram

entries.speaker: Varley
entries.label: ...: "Mister Ward,October 27th <..."
entries.text:
Mister Ward, October 27th
I'll waste no time, as there's none for wasting. I write from Blake Manor in Connemara. Yesterday, a guest went missing - a young woman named Evelyn Deane (photograph enclosed). Everyone here carries on as if nothing has happened but her room's not been slept in nor have any locals seen her off hotel grounds - she has not left, of that I am sure.
This envelope contains two-hundred pounds. Please, Sir, accept this money and come quick. I fear she's not long for this world. A further three-hundred pounds will be paid out if you find her alive.
I know the West of Ireland might well be the far side of the world for its distance from you, but there's no one else to turn to. I hear you are an honourable man, a steadfast investigator, and - perhaps most importantly - godly.
I pray for the girl that this is true. Sincerely, A concerned party.

Dear Miss Deane,
How wonderful to hear from you again! One does hear of your exploits, you know. You have quite the name for yourself in London especially. When you next find yourself in the city, you must let me show you around. You have seen much of it, I'm sure, but there are places I think will interest you it takes a most experienced eye to find! I have quite the knowledge of Dublin and London and their various sights and experiences when it comes to our less orthodox interests, I trust I can make the trip worth your while.
Do tell me when you'll have the time to meet.

title: Document Texts/Letter from Doctor Callaghan

entries.speaker: Varley

I hope you'll fo..."
entries.text:
Miss Deane,
I hope you'll forgive me the delay in reaching out to you - there has been an influx of influenza patients in Dublin, and the hospital has a great many of us working all hours.
I know my aunt has rejected your request for training in our magic, but she is overly concerned with tradition and lineages and things being done the way they have always been. I am less held by the old ways and its restrictions. Indeed, I think new paths and partnerships are required to keep the traditions alive.
I'll be attending the Grand Séance in Blake Manor, unexpected flu season or not. Let us meet there and discuss what you want to learn?
For my part, I do not ask payment for this. Instead, a favour - I intend to make inroads to the London scene and the right contacts would make it easier. Contacts I know you have.
What say you, Miss Deane? A trade?
Doctor Ruairí Callaghan.

entries.text: My Aunt might not understand that, Evelyn. But I promise you, I do.

entries.speaker: Varley
entries.label: ...: "Miss Deane, I hope you'll forgiv..."
entries.text:
Miss Deane, I hope you'll forgive me the delay in responding to your letter - there has been an influx of influenza patients in Dublin, and the hospital has a great many of us working all hours. I was rather looking forward to some time back in Connacht, but it seems that won't be on the cards for some time - so for now I remain in Dublin. I'll undoubtedly be attending this Grand Séance, unexpected flu season or not. I don't see how I could do anything else. With it so close to home, missing it is inconceivable. You are, of course, welcome to visit if you decide you wish to make more of a holiday out of your time in the county. Regarding the reception the event is getting, from what I've heard it is largely welcomed. There is some talk, as there often is, of the idea being rather too close to farming out our traditions - but it seems a hysterical opinion in this case, when séances are not in the slightest distinctly Irish. I don't disagree it could, hypothetically, become a concern, but in this case I find it baseless. The same people ought to consider, as you have said yourself, that they're very fond of Egyptian practices, these and European practices frequently being brought to London and so to Dublin. Frankly, there ought to be made some sort of consensus. Some sort of middle ground of adoption and conservation - or any sort of learned practice in these circles will become the domain of hypocrites alone. If you ask me, I think the greatest concern for all involved is not what I've outlined above, but the practising of borrowed magic without due consideration. I know you to be a sensible woman, of course, but I would worry about any peer in that Order of yours that does not properly consider the powers they wish to invoke. Or, for that matter, anyone outside of it whose interest is caught. There are those that underestimate the matters we deal with, as you well know. There is a great deal of nuance I would go on to outline, had I the time. In lieu, I hope we can discuss this when we meet for this Grand Séance instead. It will be a sincere pleasure to see you again. Yours faithfully,
Doctor Ruairí Callaghan.

entries.speaker: Varley
entries.label: ...: "Corentine is attending the Grand Sé..."
entries.text:
Corentine is attending the Grand Séance. I should have expected to see her here, of course, but she had kept such a low profile after our... disagreement.
I do regret it, of course. I should have been a more loyal friend but I had to view that book while I could. I would say that the cost to entry was too high, but I would pay it again. And again.
I didn't think she cared so much for standing. I thought she'd understand but my betrayal has clearly done more harm than anticipated. She barely acknowledged me and when I called her name, she looked at me with such anger in her eyes...
I may try again to mend things between us but she's in her books like never before. I doubt I will get near her.

entries.speaker: Varley
entries.label: ...: "Corentine is attending the Grand Sé..."
entries.text:
Corentine is attending the Grand Séance. I didn't expect to see her here. She nodded to me when she saw me, addressed me by my name, and then didn't say much at all else to me. She's in her books like never before.
I had the mind to make amends such as I could, but either she's twice as stubborn as she's ever been, or I did her more harm than I knew. It was not a pretty situation at all, but she was very clear she wants nothing more to do with me.
It's a shame. I should have liked to talk to her about this event. I'd say I miss her, but I don't want to start thinking like that, or I'll make myself sad before this event even gets going. Maybe there's nothing for it all after all, except perhaps time.

...and when I go to these things, I can't help but think that I'd like them so much more if only you'd accompany me, Cecil. Rosemary would have been the most awful play I'd ever attended if it hadn't been with you. You have a way of making the most mundane things so intriguing, so new and curiously handsome, as if under a new light entirely. You make me feel the same way, you know, when you hold me - as if I am made anew and entirely more interesting. And I know, too, that I very interesting indeed to you.
And so - for the sake of interest - do make your excuses and join me at a so-called Grand Séance in Ireland next year. Just how grand it will be remains to be seen, of course, but I think it has promise. And if it is dull, we shall just have to make our own entertainment.

October 27th.
Just my luck, that Evelyn Deane is attending this séance too. Is it too much to ask that I manage to find one such event where she is not plying her trade? Whatever that trade may be - what it is at the moment, I truly don't know. I fear if she takes to claiming to have a gift for visions, she'll become favoured for it, and I will become so obscure as to be overlooked. And what then? Visions of death and tragedy and no one to listen to them? Another ten years of suffering them quietly? I shall go mad entirely.
